message:
Please review the following document.

<document>
Grant Application: Chilled Storage for Fresh Food Distribution
Applicant: Hollins Valley Food Bank (registered charity)
To: Ashworth Community Foundation, Community Resilience Fund (capital grants)
Amount requested: £48,600

1. About us
Hollins Valley Food Bank has provided emergency food to households in the valley since 2014. We are run by two part-time paid staff and around 70 volunteers, and we operate from a warehouse in Hollinsford and three distribution sites in Hollinsford, Brackley Bridge and Over Hollins, which open on different days of the week. Referrals come from GPs, schools, Citizens Advice and the local authority's welfare team.

2. The need
Demand has risen sharply. The number of households we supported rose from an average of 410 a week in 2023 to 620 a week in 2025, an increase of 66%. Over the same period our food donations have changed in character. Supermarket surplus schemes now offer us large volumes of fresh produce, dairy and chilled ready meals, but we have no chilled storage beyond three domestic fridges, so we currently decline around 1.2 tonnes of fresh food each week. Our parcels are therefore dominated by tinned and dried goods, and clients, referrers and our own volunteers consistently tell us that families want fresh food, particularly for children.

3. The project
We are seeking funding to:
- install a 12 cubic metre walk-in cold room at our Hollinsford warehouse;
- buy a used refrigerated van, so that chilled food can be collected from supermarket depots and taken to our four distribution sites at safe temperatures;
- upgrade the warehouse electrical supply to support the cold room.

With these in place we could accept the 1.2 tonnes a week we currently decline, about 62 tonnes a year. Using the national food-redistribution conversion of 2,380 meals per tonne, that is around 147,600 additional meals a year, at a one-off capital cost of about 33p per meal in the first year alone.

4. Budget
Item | Cost
Walk-in cold room, supply and installation | £26,400
Refrigerated van (three years old, 40,000 miles) | £18,500
Electrical supply upgrade | £3,700
Total requested | £48,600

Quotes from two suppliers were obtained for the cold room and the electrical work; the lower quote is shown in each case. The van price is from a commercial dealer and includes a 12-month warranty.

5. Running costs
We have obtained estimates for the additional running costs. The cold room will add around £4,200 a year to our electricity bill. Insurance, fuel, servicing and road tax for the van will cost around £6,800 a year. Our 2025 accounts show total income of £96,000, almost all of it restricted to food purchasing and staff costs, an unrestricted surplus of £900, and unrestricted reserves of £5,100.

6. Outcomes and monitoring
We will measure:
- tonnes of fresh and chilled food received and distributed each month;
- the proportion of parcels containing fresh produce (currently under 10%; target 80% within six months);
- client feedback through our quarterly survey.
We will report to the Foundation at six and twelve months.

7. Timetable
The cold room supplier can install within eight weeks of order. We would order on award, with the cold room and van in service by October 2026.

8. Sustainability
This is a one-off capital investment. Once installed, the cold room and van will be sustainable without further grant funding, and will serve the valley for at least ten years. Our partner supermarkets have confirmed in writing that they will continue to offer us surplus fresh food.

9. Why fund us
The Foundation's Community Resilience Fund aims to strengthen local organisations' long-term capacity to meet need. This project does exactly that: a modest capital investment that permanently transforms the quality of the food we can give to families, at a very low cost per meal.
</document>
response:
# Review: Hollins Valley Food Bank Chilled Storage Application

The case for need is strong and clearly written, and the budget adds up (£26,400 + £18,500 + £3,700 = £48,600). However, there are several problems a funder would likely spot, and one of them could sink the application on its own.

## Critical issues

**1. The sustainability claim contradicts the financial information.**
Section 8 says the project "will be sustainable without further grant funding." Section 5 shows new running costs of about **£11,000 a year** (£4,200 electricity plus £6,800 van costs). Against that, the food bank has:
- an unrestricted surplus of £900
- unrestricted reserves of £5,100
- other income that is almost entirely restricted

As written, the food bank could not cover even half a year of running costs from reserves. Because the Community Resilience Fund is about *long-term capacity*, an assessor will almost certainly focus on this. The application needs a credible running-cost plan, such as:
- new unrestricted fundraising
- a sponsor for the van
- asking existing funders to vary restrictions
- savings from buying less food because more is donated

The plan should be backed by a budget, or at least by evidence such as funder letters. The sentence "sustainable without further grant funding" should be removed or substantiated.

**2. The timetable is already out of date.**
Section 7 targets service "by October 2026." That date has passed, so the timetable needs a realistic new date. It should allow for the decision period, the 8-week cold room lead time, and the electrical upgrade, which presumably must come first.

**3. The demand figure is wrong.**
A rise from 410 to 620 households a week is a **51%** increase, not 66% (210 ÷ 410 = 51.2%). An arithmetic error in the opening argument undermines confidence in the other figures, so it should be corrected.

## Inconsistencies

**4. Number of distribution sites.** Section 1 lists **three** distribution sites, but Section 3 refers to "our **four** distribution sites." Please reconcile these. If the warehouse also distributes, say so in Section 1.

**5. Asset lifespan.** Section 8 says the cold room and van "will serve the valley for at least ten years." That may be reasonable for the cold room. It is doubtful for a van that is already three years old with 40,000 miles, especially one doing regular depot runs. Either state separate lifespans or explain how the van will eventually be replaced.

## Gaps an assessor is likely to probe

**6. Chilled storage at the distribution sites.** The van keeps food cold in transit, but the sites open on different days and appear to have no refrigeration. The application doesn't explain how chilled food stays at a safe temperature once it is unloaded, or between delivery and collection. This affects both food safety and the 80% target.

**7. Food safety management.** Handling 1.2 tonnes a week of dairy and chilled ready meals is a significant step up from tinned goods. Briefly mention:
- temperature monitoring and records
- volunteer food hygiene training
- your registration with the local authority
- how you will handle short use-by dates

**8. Operational capacity.** Two part-time staff and volunteers will need to run regular depot collections, sort perishable stock and drive the van. Who will drive? Is driving a 3.5t vehicle within volunteers' licence entitlements? Is staff time needed that isn't currently funded?

**9. The 80% target.** Moving from under 10% to 80% of parcels containing fresh produce within six months is very ambitious. It depends on supermarket supply, which you don't control, and on the site-storage issue above. Consider a stepped or more modest target. Also add a measure of **spoilage or waste**, since that is a key indicator for a chilled food project.

**10. Supporting evidence.**
- The van has only one source, while the other items had two quotes. Add a second quote or explain why there isn't one.
- Attach the supermarkets' written confirmations rather than just referring to them.
- If you have survey data showing families want fresh food, include a figure. "Consistently tell us" is weaker than a number.

**11. VAT.** State whether the costs include VAT. Charities often can't recover it, and funders want to know the budget is complete.

## Minor points

- The cost-per-meal calculation is correct: 62 t × 2,380 = about 147,600 meals, and £48,600 ÷ 147,600 = about 33p. However, "in the first year alone" is ambiguous, and the figure excludes running costs. Including the £11,000 a year would be more honest and still looks good (about 7p per meal ongoing). Also name the source of the conversion factor (WRAP).
- Section 9 says the investment "permanently transforms" provision. Given issues 1 and 5, soften this wording.

## Summary

| Priority | Fix |
|---|---|
| Must | Running-cost funding plan; remove or substantiate the "sustainable" claim |
| Must | Update the timetable |
| Must | Correct 66% to 51% |
| Should | Reconcile three vs four sites; revise the van lifespan |
| Should | Address storage at the sites, food safety, drivers and capacity |
| Should | Add a second van quote, supermarket letters, a waste metric and VAT status |
| Could | Revise the 80% target; refine the cost-per-meal wording |

With the running-cost question answered convincingly, this would be a compelling application. Without it, the request risks looking like it creates a liability the organisation can't afford.
